before:

  • Traffic camera data is purged (days to weeks)

after:
• Surveillance footage is overwritten, often within days
  • Traffic camera footage, if recorded at all, is not kept long
  • Dashcam and engine data have no federal retention rule; truck ELD logs need be kept only six months (49 C.F.R. § 395.8(k))
  • Vehicle damage is repaired or the car is scrapped
  • Road conditions change (potholes fixed, signs added, construction completed)

before:

before: For car accidents and most injury cases, the discovery rule does NOT apply — you know you're injured on the day of the crash.
after: In a car accident the rule usually changes nothing: you know you were hurt on the day of the crash — and an injury that later worsens does not restart the clock (Dean v. Ruscon Corp., 1996).

before:
• Minor plaintiff: If the injured person is under 18, the clock doesn't start until they turn 18
  • Defendant absent from state: If the at-fault party leaves South Carolina, time may toll during their absence
  • Mental incapacity: If the injury rendered the plaintiff mentally incapacitated
after:
• Minor plaintiff: If under 18, the deadline is generally the 19th birthday, or three years from the injury if later (S.C. Code § 15-3-40)
  • Defendant absent from state: If the at-fault party moves out of state, or is away a year or more, that time may not count (S.C. Code § 15-3-30)
  • Mental incapacity: If legally incompetent when the claim arises, the clock pauses for at most five years and at most one year after it ends (S.C. Code §§ 15-3-40, 15-3-50)

before: The statute requires that your lawsuit be filed with the court — not that settlement negotiations be ongoing, not that you've hired an attorney, not that you've sent a demand letter. The Summons and Complaint must be filed with the Clerk of Court before the 3-year anniversary of your injury.
after: The statute requires that your lawsuit be filed with the court — not that settlement negotiations be ongoing, not that you've hired an attorney, not that you've sent a demand letter. The Summons and Complaint must be filed with the Clerk of Court before the 3-year anniversary of your injury, and the defendant must be served within 120 days after filing (S.C. Code § 15-3-20(B)).

before: South Carolina gives personal injury victims 3 years from the date of injury to file a lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Exceptions include: 2-year deadline for claims against government entities under the SC Tort Claims Act, tolling for minors (deadline paused until age 18), and the discovery rule (clock starts when the injury is or should have been discovered). Waiting to file weakens cases — evidence degrades, witnesses forget, and defendants destroy records.
after: South Carolina gives personal injury victims 3 years from the date of injury to file a lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Exceptions include: 2-year deadline for claims against government entities under the SC Tort Claims Act (no notice required; 3 years with an optional verified claim filed within 1 year), tolling for minors (generally until one year after the child turns 18), and the discovery rule (the clock runs from when you knew or should have known you had a claim, S.C. Code § 15-3-535; in a crash, usually the crash date). Waiting to file weakens cases — evidence degrades, witnesses forget, and records can be lawfully discarded or overwritten.
South Carolina gives injury victims 3 years to sue (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Learn the exceptions: government claims, minors, discovery and tolling.

before: Your claim is permanently barred, no matter how serious your injuries or how clear the other driver's fault was. A court does not weigh the merits of a claim filed out of time, so the deadline is effectively absolute.
after: Your claim is permanently barred, no matter how serious your injuries or how clear the other driver's fault was. Unless a tolling rule applies, a court will dismiss a claim filed out of time without weighing its merits.
